chapter_theme: Civakan makes a garland that the maid carries to Kanakamalai; the princess, wasting with love, laments to the evening, the cuckoo and her own life, says she sold her modesty for a garland, and sends her own garland back, which Civakan after a scruple accepts as the work of former deed; the maid's cooling remedies fail and only his garland comforts her, while the princes finish their training in arms.

cast.role: the hero, teaching the princes arms; called நம்பி and பெருந்தகை here
the princess who falls in love with Civakan
the cuckoo of the grove whom Kanakamalai reproaches
the young princes Civakan is training in arms

1653.reading: Civakan, whose shining teeth are like a lion cub's, makes a garland and a flower-ball from honeyed blossoms, steeps them in perfume and sprinkles musk, and then a serving woman of milk-sweet speech comes, bees humming about her, and bows to him.
1653.event: Civakan makes a perfumed garland and flower-ball, and Kanakamalai's maid comes and bows to him.
1653.nuance: The garland is Civakan's own work (the princess later calls it the one he himself made, 1663); the maid is named only at 1668.

1654.reading: The maid says that eyes cannot blink before such things and that they suit her mistress, Civakan tells her to take them, and she carries them to the princess, bows and shows them, and the princess takes them.
1654.event: The maid asks for the garland for her mistress, Civakan gives it, and Kanakamalai receives it.
1654.nuance: Line 1 (வாயா இமைப்பு) is hard to construe; the reading that the maid praises the work so that the eye cannot close is mine.

1655.reading: Holding the garland with its flower-lettering on her soft fingers, the princess gazes at it while bees settle on her hair and drip honey, and the narrator says that those who have not seen the dance of her spear-like eyes live a life no better than hill hunters'.
1655.event: Kanakamalai holds Civakan's garland and gazes at it.
1655.nuance: மலரெழுத்து suggests the garland carries letters worked in flowers, a message as well as a gift.

1656.reading: The narrator gives the common saying that for women with coral lips, nectar-sweet and with hips like a hooded serpent, daily union on a cool flower bed makes their bamboo-soft shoulders grow in beauty.
1656.nuance: என்ப, 'they say', marks this and 1657 as received wisdom about love set in the narrative pause.

1657.reading: The narrator turns the woman's body into a dice game, chest as the gem board, breasts as dice and hips as the gaming hall, and says that if this headlong game of love cannot be played, then restraint won by penance is, as they say, the beauty of manliness.

claims.claim: when love's pleasure is not to be had, restraint gained through penance is what becomes a man

1657.nuance: The maxim is general, not tied to a school in the verse, though penance (நோற்று) and restraint are the Jain epic's later end for Civakan; it sits between the princess receiving the garland and her lament, as if a comment on Civakan's hesitation.

1658.reading: The princess sits with thighs like an elephant's trunk under a fine cloth, earrings and gold ear-discs glittering, her neck tilted, unblinking, lost in thought, like a yakshi seated in beauty.
1658.event: Kanakamalai sits motionless, thinking of Civakan.
1658.nuance: இமையாள், unblinking, is the mark of a goddess or yakshi, and the simile completes it: love has fixed her like an image.

1659.reading: Like a young doe struck by a fierce hunter's arrow, she is shaken, her bangled arms grow thin, her shoulders waste and pallor spreads over her breasts, and the peacock-like girl speaks thus to her own heart.
1659.event: Kanakamalai wastes with longing and begins to speak to her heart.

1660.reading: She sees the evening as a great one-toothed demon gaping to swallow the world, the long white moon its gleaming tooth and the red sky its bloody mouth, come today to swallow her, and asks what will become of her pitiable life.

1661.reading: She tells the dark cuckoo of the grove that the mother who bore it forgot it and the one who reared it drove it from the house, so who would scold it, yet it never says this is wrong or that her life will perish, but sits and calls on.
1661.nuance: The cuckoo raised by another bird (the crow, not named) is reproached as one without kin to teach it pity, so its call is heartless.

1662.reading: With the great white moon, the jasmine evening, the anril's call and the ambal's scent all moving upon her life, she, one woman, finds the whole world her enemy, and tells her life that it stays on like an offering set out for the fire to take.
1662.nuance: Lines 2 and 4 are hard to divide; பாகை is read here as பகை, and எரிகொன்று ஈன்ற இலைப்பலி is construed only roughly.

1663.reading: Her heart burns, her body is fevered, her breath comes hot and leaving, flower-haired women look at her and laugh until she is a thing to laugh at, and alone with no one she will swim the sea of the night with the cool garland the hero made as her raft.

1664.reading: The narrator says the moon-faced girl, whose long streaked eyes outdo Murugan's red spear and the flower arrows from Kama's bow, was like a flowering branch, fragrant and dripping honey, caught in a fierce fire.

1665.reading: She says she sold her dark gem-like colour, her softness, her bangles and the precious modesty that was her covering, and bought with them a garland of many flowers, while the great bee of slander hums about her.
1665.nuance: Love is told as a bargain: modesty, called her mantle (போர்வை), is the price, and the gossip (புறஞ்சொல்) is its cost; the garland is all she has in return.

1666.reading: Her young parrot tells her not to grieve, since the garland was strung of flowers by a girl whose eyes spread wide as her lover's love, as though asking whether a thing made of flowers (அலர்) could fail to become talk (அலர்), and so comforts her.
1666.event: Kanakamalai's parrot speaks to comfort her.
1666.nuance: The verse turns on அலர் as flower and as gossip; whether the parrot says the talk will cease or that it cannot be helped depends on how ஒழியுமே is taken, and who strung the garland (line 2) is unclear.

1667.reading: She says that he has bound her heart and stolen her beauty and she too will bind him, gives the maid a lasting garland from her gem casket to take to him, and the maid takes it with joined hands and goes swan-like, anklets ringing, until she reaches him.
1667.event: Kanakamalai sends her own garland to Civakan by the maid.
1667.nuance: பிணித்து / பிணிப்பேன: the garland that bound her is to be answered by a garland that binds him, so the exchange of flowers is an exchange of bonds.

1668.reading: Anangavilasini stands before him, joins her palms and holds out the garland, and when the noble one does not take it but looks at her face, she tells him that he strings garlands for her peerless peacock's hand, he is the medicine for her shoulders and her very life, so let him take it.
1668.event: The maid offers Kanakamalai's garland; Civakan hesitates and she presses him.
1668.nuance: Civakan's hesitation is the first sign that taking the garland means more than a courtesy.

1669.reading: She laughs at him, asking why he fears when those who live in kings' palaces keep their seals of honour, and he answers that it is not that, but that such a course does not suit him; then, thinking that the swan-gaited girl will suffer, he agrees.
1669.event: Civakan, teased by the maid, says secret love is not his way but consents for the princess's sake.

claims.claim: secret dealings in love do not befit him

1669.nuance: The split of the dialogue is my reading: the line on palace dwellers with sealed honour (பொறி செறித்த மாண்பினர்) may instead be his scruple and the laughter hers; கோதாய் addresses the maid. He yields from pity for her pain, not from desire.

1670.reading: He holds out his lotus-like hand and takes the garland, saying it comes by former deed and burns the heart, and the maid goes off and begins the means by which Kanakamalai, wasting and fevered, may be saved.
1670.event: Civakan accepts Kanakamalai's garland and the maid begins remedies for her.

claims.claim: love's burning comes as the fruit of a former deed

1670.nuance: Who says இஃது ஊழ்வினையால் உள்ளஞ் சுடும் is not clear: Civakan as he accepts, or the maid of the princess's fever; the claim is given to Civakan on the first reading. Either way the love is put down to ஊழ்வினை while Civakan's own consent was shown in 1669, so destiny and choice are both given.

1671.reading: She lays on the princess moonstone that sheds water, fragrant sandal, blossoms of kazhuneer, lotus bracelets on thongs and water from a white mountain waterfall, and none of them cool her.
1671.event: The maid applies cooling things to Kanakamalai, without effect.
1671.nuance: Line 2 begins with a doubtful syllable in the edition (printed with a query), and the opening words of line 1 divide uncertainly.

1672.reading: She also fastens on her a rare gem born in the sea, cool and able to drive off heat, worth the world for which kings suffer, worked on a fine thread, and still more such things on the fragrant-haired girl.
1672.event: The maid puts a cooling sea-gem on Kanakamalai.
1672.nuance: பனிபெயர்க்கும் may mean the gem removes affliction or sheds coolness; the reading is uncertain.

1673.reading: She lets fragrant water fall over garlands, makes a cool flower couch below them, fans her with a moist fan and a golden round fan, and smears her whole body with rich cool sandal paste.
1673.event: The maid makes Kanakamalai a flower bed, fans her and covers her in sandal.

1674.reading: The sandal on her breasts does not cool them but withers her life, the soft garlands blacken and drip, and only the bright garland the hero strung becomes the companion and raft of the girl with heavy hair.
1674.nuance: Every remedy fails and the only relief is the token of the one who causes the fever: the garland is both the sickness and its cure, as the maid called him her medicine in 1668.

1675.reading: While long-eyed Kanakamalai passes her days with the maid as her messenger and the garland as her raft, the young men reach the farther shore of the faultless sea of learning.
1675.event: Kanakamalai's love continues through the maid, and the princes complete their training under Civakan.
1675.nuance: One verse joins the two threads: her sea of night (1663) and the princes' sea of learning, both crossed, hers only with a raft of flowers.

1676.reading: Civakan shows them in full how to drive the fighting arrow and the dart, how to ward off a coming arrow, how to swim through sword battle, how to hide within armour and how to see an arrow's back, and even those who sat in state learned.
1676.event: The princes learn the arts of weapons from Civakan.
1676.nuance: வீற்றிருந்தவரும் கற்றார் may mean the king and elders seated in state learned too, or that the princes learned while sitting at ease; கருவியுட் கரக்கும் ஆறு is read as hiding within one's gear.

links.note: Her resolve to bind him with her garland is fulfilled when he takes it.
links.teaches: Together they show the binding she plans in private take effect only through his hesitant consent, so the exchange of garlands becomes a mutual tie rather than her gift alone.

links.note: The hero's garland as her raft: first in her own lament, then in the narrator's account of failed remedies.
links.teaches: The raft she claims in despair in 1663 is confirmed by the narrator in 1674 after every cooling remedy fails, so the image moves from a lover's hope to the story's fact.

links.note: Love explained by a former deed: Civakan's father ran after his queen because an earlier disposition sprouted; Civakan takes the garland saying it comes by ūzhvinai.
links.teaches: Set beside the father's fatal infatuation, which the narrator blames on former deed, the son's acceptance under the same explanation shows the epic marking each of his loves as karma at work, but here with a pause of scruple the father never had.

links.note: The raft (புணை) on the deep sea: in 380 the Wise One to whom the youth goes for refuge, here the hero's garland on the sea of night.
links.teaches: The Jain epic uses one image for refuge from the sea of births and for a girl's hold on her lover's token, so the reader sees desire offering a false copy of the refuge the teacher gives.

links.note: The Kural's woman says there is a sea of love but no safe raft to cross it; Kanakamalai finds her raft in the garland Civakan made.
links.teaches: The pair shows that the raft the couplet denies can be supplied by a token of the beloved, but only as a raft through the night, not a way out of the sea.

gains.a: the epic's raft is read against a known claim that love has none, which makes the garland's comfort pointed
gains.b: the couplet's abstract missing raft is given a concrete candidate, a love gift, and the epic's later failures of cooling test whether it holds

links.note: Both women swim love's flood alone in the night watches (யாமம்).
links.teaches: Where the couplet's woman sees no shore and is simply alone, the epic adds the watchers who laugh at her, so the solitude of the night becomes public shame by day.

gains.a: Kanakamalai's 'sea of the night' is placed in the Kural's convention of the midnight flood of love
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'I alone' gains a social side, the women who mock the lovesick girl

links.note: The Kural's lover says love's flood carries off the raft of modesty and manliness; Kanakamalai says she sold her modesty to buy a garland.
links.teaches: The epic turns the couplet's loss into a trade: modesty is not swept away but given in exchange, and what it bought, the garland, becomes the new raft of 1663 and 1674.

gains.a: her bargain is read as the woman's version of the loss the Kural gives to a man
gains.b: the couplet's image gains a sequel in which the lost raft of modesty is replaced by one of love

links.note: Evening as what eats the lives of the separated: the couplet's woman says it is not evening but the hour that devours; Kanakamalai sees it as a demon gaping to swallow her.
links.teaches: The epic makes the couplet's figure of devouring evening into a visible monster, the moon its tooth and the red sky its mouth, showing how a Kural conceit was expanded into scenery.

gains.a: her terror of evening is placed in the Kural's convention of the devouring hour
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'eats life' is given a body and features drawn from the evening sky

links.note: The Kural condemns those who clung to dice (கவறு) and the gaming hall (கழகம); the epic makes the woman's body a board, dice and gaming hall for love.
links.teaches: Borrowing the Kural's own words for ruinous gambling, the epic frames love as a game one should give up for penance when it cannot be won, so the condemned dice become a figure for the pleasure renunciation replaces.

gains.a: the conceit's choice of dice gains the Kural's moral weight against gaming, which prepares its turn to restraint
gains.b: the Kural's dice and hall are shown entering a love conceit, a use the couplet does not foresee

links.note: The Kural's lover says he once had modesty and manliness and now has only the palmyra horse; the epic's maxim says restraint is the beauty of manliness when love fails.
links.teaches: Against the Kural's man who says love has taken his manliness, the epic defines manliness as the restraint that remains when love is denied, so the same word marks opposite outcomes of desire.

gains.a: the epic's maxim is seen as a reply to the Kural's account of love overcoming manliness
gains.b: the couplet's despair is set against a path the lover does not consider, restraint through penance

source_issues: Most verses (all but 1657, 1671, 1675) were printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 by the build.
1671 line 1 ends with a query mark (அழகியவோ?) in the edition; the line 1/2 boundary there is doubtful.
1662 lines 2-4 and 1654 line 1: word division unclear, sense uncertain.
1669: the edition does not mark where the maid's words end and Civakan's begin.
